topics.title: Pressure Injuries: What They Are, How They Form & Who Is at Risk
topics.summary: Prolonged pressure over a bony prominence squeezes off blood flow until tissue starves and dies — and some clients (immobile, poorly nourished, incontinent, confused, numb, febrile, older, chronically ill) get there much faster than others.
objectives: After this lesson you can explain, step by step, how prolonged pressure turns healthy tissue into an open ulcer.
Name the bony prominences where pressure injuries form most often and link each to the position that loads it.
Tell the difference between pressure, friction, and shear, and give a bedside example of each.
List every risk factor from the slides and explain WHY each one raises risk.
Interpret a Braden scale score, remembering that a LOWER score means HIGHER risk, and use subscale scores to target care.
topics.bigPicture:
A pressure injury can start in less time than a movie lasts. When a client lies or sits in one position without moving, the body's own weight presses the skin and the tissue under it against the bed or chair. The tiny blood vessels in that squeezed tissue close off. No blood means no oxygen and no nutrients, and tissue that goes without them long enough dies.

Here is the hopeful part: most pressure injuries are preventable. The nurse is the person best placed to spot which clients are at risk and to stop the chain of events before the skin breaks down. To do that, you need to understand how the injury forms and what makes some clients so much more vulnerable than others.

keyTerms.def: Localized damage to the skin and the tissue under it, usually over a bony prominence, caused by prolonged pressure (sometimes combined with friction or shear). Also called a bedsore, pressure ulcer, or decubitus ulcer.
A place where bone sits close under the skin with little padding — for example the sacrum, heels, hips, and ischia.
Not enough blood flow to a tissue, so it is short of oxygen and nutrients.
Death of cells or tissue. Necrotic tissue cannot recover; it must be removed or break down.
An open sore where the skin (and sometimes deeper tissue) has broken down and been lost.
The pressure of blood inside the smallest vessels — about 32 mm Hg. Outside pressure higher than this, if it lasts, squeezes the capillaries shut.
Rubbing of the skin against a surface (like a sheet) that scrapes the outer skin layer.
A sliding force: the skin stays stuck to the surface while the bones and deeper tissue slide the other way, stretching and tearing deep blood vessels.
Softening and breakdown of skin that has stayed wet too long (think of "pruney" fingers after a long bath).
Wasting or shrinking of muscle or tissue, which removes padding over bone.
Nerve damage that reduces feeling, often in the feet and legs (common in diabetes).
A standard tool that scores six areas (sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction & shear) to predict pressure injury risk. Total 6–23; lower = higher risk.
Another pressure-injury risk tool the slides name; like Braden, a lower score means higher risk.

sections.heading: What a pressure injury is — and why it matters
sections.body:
A pressure injury is damage to the skin and the tissue beneath it caused by prolonged pressure. You will also hear older names: bedsore, pressure ulcer, and decubitus ulcer ("decubitus" comes from Latin for "lying down"). All of these mean the same thing on an exam.

Pressure injuries are common. According to your slides, up to about 29% of hospitalized clients develop one, and 2.6–24% of long-term care residents do. In home care, the number is probably underreported — family caregivers may not recognize early damage — and it is a growing concern as more people receive care at home.

A pressure injury causes pain, can become infected, and can take weeks or months to heal — which is why prevention matters so much.
sections.analogy: Think of a garden hose lying across your driveway. If a car parks on it for a moment, water still gets through once the car moves. If the car parks there all day, the plants at the end of the hose wilt and die. The client's body weight is the car, the capillaries are the hose, and the skin and tissue are the plants.

sections.heading: How the damage happens: pressure → ischemia → necrosis → ulcer
sections.body:
Blood reaches the skin through capillaries, tiny vessels with thin walls. The pressure of blood inside them is only about 32 mm Hg. That is low. When a client lies on a firm mattress, the pressure under a bony spot like the sacrum can easily go higher than that. When outside pressure is greater than capillary pressure, the capillaries are squeezed flat and blood stops flowing through them.

Healthy people shift position constantly because squeezed tissue feels uncomfortable. But when pressure lasts, the tissue runs out of oxygen and nutrients (ischemia). Waste products build up. If pressure is not relieved, the cells die (necrosis). Dead tissue breaks down, and an open sore forms (ulcer).

Notice that the damage often starts deep, next to the bone, where the tissue is squeezed hardest. The skin on top may look only a little red while deeper tissue is already dying. That is why early signs must be taken seriously.
steps: Prolonged pressure compresses tissue between the bone and the bed or chair.
Blood flow through the compressed capillaries decreases (outside pressure > about 32 mm Hg).
The tissue becomes ischemic — starved of oxygen and nutrients.
Cells in the ischemic tissue die (necrosis).
The dead tissue breaks down, forming an open ulcer.

check.q: A client was found on the floor after lying on the right side for 10 hours. The right hip is red and does not blanch. In one sentence, explain what happened to the tissue.
check.a: Body weight pushed external pressure above capillary pressure (about 32 mm Hg), blood flow stopped, the tissue became ischemic, and if unrelieved it will undergo necrosis and may break down into an ulcer.

sections.heading: Where pressure injuries form: the bony prominences
sections.body:
Pressure injuries form where bone is close to the skin and there is little fat or muscle to cushion it. The slides name the classic sites: heels, sacrum (the triangle-shaped bone at the base of the spine), hips (the greater trochanter — the bony knob on the side of the upper thigh), and ischia (the "sit bones," or ischial tuberosities, that you sit on).

Which spots are at risk depends on the client's position. Whatever part of the body is carrying the weight is the part in danger. Use the table below whenever you plan skin inspections.

table.caption: Pressure points by position
rows: Occiput (back of head), scapulae (shoulder blades), elbows, sacrum and coccyx, heels
Ear, shoulder, greater trochanter (hip), knees (inner surfaces touching), ankles
Forehead and chin, chest, iliac crests, anterior knees, toes
Ischial tuberosities (sit bones), sacrum/coccyx, heels or feet

sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. D has been lying on his back most of the shift. Which areas do you inspect most closely? The occiput, scapulae, sacrum and coccyx, and heels — the prominences that carry weight in the supine position. The anterior knees and forehead are prone pressure points, so they are not the priority for him right now.

sections.heading: Friction and shear: the sliding forces
sections.body:
The slides point out that pressure injuries may also come from friction or shearing forces. These often add to the damage that pressure has started.

Friction is rubbing. When a client is dragged up in bed, the sheet scrapes the skin, removing the top layer like sandpaper. This leaves a raw area that breaks down more easily.

Shear is sneakier and deeper. Picture a client sitting with the head of the bed (HOB) raised high. Gravity pulls the body down toward the foot of the bed. The skin over the sacrum sticks to the sheet, but the skeleton keeps sliding. The layers between skin and bone are stretched in opposite directions, which kinks and tears the small blood vessels deep inside. The skin may look fine at first, while deep tissue is badly damaged.

This is why the prevention slides tell you to keep the HOB at 30° or lower when possible and to use draw sheets or lifts instead of dragging clients.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. L has heart failure and likes the HOB at 60°. Every hour she has slid toward the foot of the bed. What worries you most? Shear injury over the sacrum. Her skin stays fixed to the sheet while her skeleton slides down. You would lift (not drag) her back up with a draw sheet and a second person, and keep the HOB as low as her breathing allows (ideally ≤ 30°).

sections.heading: Risk factors, part 1: can the client feel it, move away from it, and feed the tissue?
sections.body: Anyone can get a pressure injury, but certain factors make it much more likely. For each one, ask yourself why it raises risk — exam questions often test the reasoning, not just the list.
bullets: Immobility — from paralysis, weakness, pain, or sedation. A client who cannot move cannot relieve pressure. Pain makes clients reluctant to move; sedation takes away the urge to move at all.

Inadequate nutrition — too little protein, calories, zinc, and vitamin C. The result is weight loss (less fat padding over bone), muscle atrophy (less muscle padding), and edema (swollen tissue that is poorly oxygenated and fragile). Poorly nourished tissue also cannot repair itself.

Incontinence — urine and stool bring moisture, enzymes, and urea to the skin. Wet skin softens (maceration), and enzymes in stool literally digest the skin. The result is skin breakdown and a higher chance of infection.
Decreased mental status — a confused, sedated, or unconscious client may not notice pain or pressure, or may not know to respond to it by moving or asking for help.
Diminished sensation — from paralysis, stroke, neuropathy, or aging. These clients cannot feel the early warning signs (discomfort) that would normally make them shift position.
sections.example: At the bedside: Four clients: (1) a 45-year-old with a wrist cast who walks and eats all meals; (2) a 29-year-old with a new T4 spinal cord injury, a fever of 38.9 °C, and bowel incontinence; (3) a 70-year-old with heart failure who walks the halls three times a day; (4) a 62-year-old with diabetes who sits in a chair but shifts on their own. Who is at greatest risk? Client 2 — no sensation and no movement below the injury, plus fever and moisture. Risk climbs steeply when several factors stack together.

sections.heading: Risk factors, part 2: heat, age, chronic disease, and how we handle the client
bullets: Excessive body heat (fever) — heat raises the metabolic rate, so cells need more oxygen. Tissue under pressure is already short of oxygen, so a hotter, hungrier tissue becomes ischemic faster.

Advanced age — older skin is thinner and less elastic, has less oil, poorer circulation, and is drier. It tears and breaks down more easily and heals more slowly. Many older adults also have several of the other risk factors.
Chronic medical conditions — diabetes and cardiovascular disease reduce circulation and delay healing, so tissue tolerates pressure poorly and recovers slowly.

Other contributing factors (these are about care, and nurses control them!): poor lifting and transferring techniques, incorrect positioning, hard support surfaces, and incorrect use of pressure-relieving devices.
sections.body: The last group is worth pausing on. A client can be low-risk on paper and still be injured by the way staff move them, the surface they lie on, or a device that is used wrong (for example, a doughnut cushion, or a specialty mattress piled with folded pads). Good technique is part of prevention.

check.q: A student asks why a fever of 39.2 °C raises the risk of a pressure injury. What do you say?
check.a: Fever raises the metabolic rate and oxygen demand, so tissue that is already squeezed over a bony prominence becomes ischemic faster.

sections.heading: Measuring risk: the Braden scale (and Norton)
sections.body:
The slides call for a baseline risk assessment using a tool such as the Braden or Norton scale. The Braden scale is the one you will see most. It scores six areas that match the risk factors you just learned:

Sensory perception (can the client feel and respond to discomfort?), moisture (how often is the skin wet?), activity (bedfast, chairfast, walks?), mobility (can the client change position?), nutrition (usual intake), and friction & shear (does the client slide or need to be dragged?). The first five are scored 1–4; friction & shear is scored 1–3. The total runs from 6 to 23.

The big trap: Braden runs "backwards." A LOW score means HIGH risk. A 1 in any area is the worst possible score for that area.

Use the subscales to target care. A client might total 19 (looks "not at risk") yet score 1 on moisture because of constant incontinence. That one area needs action now: prompt cleansing and a barrier cream. The Braden scale predicts risk; it does not diagnose or stage an injury that is already there.

table.caption: Braden total score (commonly used cutoffs — your textbook may vary slightly)

sections.example: At the bedside: A 79-year-old after hip repair responds only to painful stimuli, is on bed rest, eats about a third of meals, is often incontinent of urine, and slides down when the HOB is raised. Braden total = 11. Interpretation: high risk. Every subscale is pulling the score down — sensation, activity, nutrition, moisture, friction & shear — so each needs a matching intervention.

mnemonics.name: "Feel it, move it, wet it, feed it"
mnemonics.text: Four quick questions that cover most risk: Can the client FEEL pressure? MOVE away from it? Is the skin WET? Is the tissue FED (nutrition)?

pearls: Braden is inverse: LOW score = HIGH risk. The range is 6–23.
Look at subscales, not just the total — one subscale of 1 needs a targeted intervention even if the total looks safe.
HOB raised + client sliding down = sacral SHEAR (deep tissue damage), not just friction.
Fever is a risk factor because it raises oxygen demand; don't overlook it in a pneumonia or post-op client.
On "who is at greatest risk?" questions, pick the client with the most risk factors stacked together — especially lost sensation plus immobility.
redFlags: New redness over a bony prominence that does not fade after pressure is relieved → keep the client off it and assess further (possible Stage I).
Sudden drop in Braden score (sedation, surgery, new incontinence, fever) → increase turning, skin checks, and moisture control this shift.
Client sliding down in bed with HOB high → lift (don't drag) back up and lower the HOB if allowed to reduce shear.
recap: Pressure injury = damage from prolonged pressure; also called bedsore, pressure ulcer, decubitus ulcer.
Pathway: pressure → ↓ blood flow → ischemia → necrosis → ulcer.
Common sites: heels, sacrum, hips (trochanters), ischia — whatever bone bears weight.
Friction scrapes the surface; shear tears deep vessels when the body slides but the skin doesn't.
Risk factors: immobility, poor nutrition, incontinence, decreased mental status, diminished sensation, fever, advanced age, chronic disease, and poor handling/surfaces/devices.
Braden score 6–23: lower = higher risk; use subscales to target care.
Incidence: up to 29% in hospitals, 2.6–24% in long-term care, underreported at home.

checks.q: Put these in order: necrosis, ↓ blood flow, ulcer, prolonged pressure, ischemia.
checks.a: Prolonged pressure → ↓ blood flow → ischemia → necrosis → ulcer.

checks.q: A client with dementia is incontinent of stool, eats 25% of meals, and needs help to move. Name three risk factors and why each matters.
checks.a: Decreased mental status (can't sense or respond to pressure), incontinence (moisture and enzymes macerate skin), inadequate nutrition (less padding and poor repair); immobility as well.

checks.q: A client's Braden total is 19, but moisture is scored 1. What is the priority?
checks.a: Manage moisture — prompt gentle cleansing and a barrier cream — because a single worst-possible subscale is a real risk even when the total looks reassuring.

checks.q: Why can a client with a spinal cord injury develop a deep pressure injury without complaining?
checks.a: Diminished sensation — they cannot feel the discomfort that normally warns a person to shift position.

topics.title: Preventing Pressure Injuries: Nutrition, Skin Care, Repositioning & Support Devices
topics.summary: Most pressure injuries are preventable: feed the tissue, keep the skin clean and dry, move the client on schedule without dragging, and use support devices the right way.
objectives: After this lesson you can name the key nutrients for skin integrity and the lab values that track nutritional status.
Describe safe skin hygiene, including what products to use and what to avoid.
State the repositioning times for a client in bed, in a chair, and for self weight shifts.
Explain why HOB ≤ 30°, draw sheets, and smooth firm surfaces reduce injury.
Choose appropriate support devices, explain the 32 mm Hg goal, and explain why doughnut devices are avoided.
topics.bigPicture:
Prevention is where nurses make the biggest difference. Every item on the prevention slides fights one of the causes you learned about: good nutrition builds stronger tissue, skin hygiene protects against moisture and enzymes, repositioning relieves pressure before tissue dies, and support devices spread weight out so no single spot is crushed.

These are everyday nursing actions — many are done by assistive personnel under your direction — but doing them the right way matters. A turn done by dragging the client, a doughnut cushion, hot water, or powder can cause the very injury you are trying to prevent.

Exams love prevention questions because they test judgment: "Which action needs correction?" "Which statement shows the caregiver needs more teaching?" Learn the why behind each rule and you will spot the wrong answer quickly.

keyTerms.def: A main blood protein. A low level suggests poor protein nutrition (and is linked to edema and slow healing).
A type of white blood cell; a low count can reflect poor nutrition and weak immune defenses.
Extra nutrition (e.g., a high-protein, high-calorie shake) given when meals alone are not enough.
A product (such as dimethicone or an alcohol-free spray) that forms a protective layer between skin and moisture.
A sheet placed under the client's trunk so two staff can LIFT the client up or over instead of dragging.
A side-lying position partway toward prone, with the top leg bent forward.
Side-lying tilted only about 30° (supported by pillows) so weight rests on the buttock muscle instead of the hip bone or sacrum.
A foam or gel pad placed on top of a standard mattress to spread out pressure.
A specialty bed with air-filled cushions that redistribute pressure and let air flow to keep skin cooler and drier.
A specialty bed that slowly rotates the client side to side.
To take pressure completely off a body part (e.g., "floating" the heels off the bed).

sections.heading: Prevention pillar 1: Nutrition — feed the tissue
sections.body:
The slide says it plainly: adequate intake = fewer pressure injuries. Well-nourished tissue has more padding, stronger skin, and the building blocks to repair small damage before it becomes a wound.

The key nutrients are protein (the building block of new tissue), calories (energy; without enough, the body burns its own protein), vitamin A (supports new skin cells and healing), vitamin C (needed to make collagen, the "scaffolding" of skin and scar tissue), zinc (helps cells divide and repair), and iron (needed for hemoglobin to carry oxygen to tissues). Adequate fluids keep skin supple too.

To track whether nutrition is adequate, the slides tell you to monitor weight, lymphocyte count, albumin, and hemoglobin. Unplanned weight loss, low albumin, low hemoglobin, or low lymphocytes all suggest the client is nutritionally compromised. If they are, use supplements (for example, high-protein shakes between meals) and consult the registered dietitian.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mrs. P, 68, has a sacral wound, lost 5 kg over 6 weeks, eats about half of each meal, and has an albumin of 2.9 g/dL (low). What do you do? Encourage protein and foods rich in vitamin C (for collagen), vitamin A, zinc, and iron; offer high-protein, high-calorie supplements between meals; trend weight, albumin, hemoglobin, and lymphocytes; and request a dietitian consult. Restricting fluids or protein would be wrong — the tissue needs more, not less.

check.q: Which vitamin is especially linked to collagen formation?
check.a: Vitamin C — collagen is the structural protein of skin and healing tissue.

sections.heading: Prevention pillar 2: Skin hygiene — clean, dry, moisturized, protected
sections.body:
Start with a baseline risk assessment (Braden scale or similar) so you know how aggressive prevention must be. Then inspect the skin: in the hospital, twice daily; in home care, weekly (more often for higher-risk clients). Focus on the bony prominences.

Cleanse gently with mild agents and avoid hot water. Hot water and harsh soaps strip away the skin's natural oils and damage fragile skin, especially in older adults. Pat dry — do not rub, because rubbing is friction.

Keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized. That sounds contradictory, but it isn't: dry means no pooled moisture from urine, stool, sweat, or wound drainage; moisturized means not cracked and flaky. Apply lotion to dry skin, and use a barrier cream or film (such as dimethicone or an alcohol-free spray) where moisture is a problem, like the perineum of an incontinent client.

Avoid petroleum ointments, baby powder, and cornstarch. Powders and cornstarch clump when wet, creating gritty, irritating paste in skin folds (cornstarch can also feed yeast). Petroleum-based ointments are listed on your slides as products to avoid as well.
steps: Perform hand hygiene, apply clean gloves, and remove the soiled pad promptly.
Cleanse the skin gently with a mild cleanser and warm (not hot) water.
Pat the skin dry without rubbing.
Apply a thin layer of barrier cream (e.g., dimethicone).
Place a single breathable underpad (not a stack) and reposition the client off the sacrum.

check.q: A UAP plans to dust cornstarch into a client's skin folds and bathe the client in hot water "to stimulate circulation." Should you intervene?
check.a: Yes — both are on the "avoid" list: cornstarch clumps and irritates, and hot water dries and damages fragile skin.

sections.heading: Prevention pillar 3: Repositioning — move them before the tissue runs out of time
sections.body:
Repositioning is the single most direct way to relieve pressure. The slides give three time frames — memorize them as a set:

• Bedbound clients: reposition at least every 2 hours.
• Clients sitting in a chair: reposition every 1 hour (from the implementation slide). Sitting puts the whole upper body's weight on the small ischial tuberosities, so the chair is actually riskier than the bed.
• Clients who can move themselves: shift weight every 15–30 minutes (the implementation slide says teach weight shifting every 15 minutes). This can be a wheelchair push-up, leaning side to side, or leaning forward.

Rotate through the positions the slides list: prone, supine, right and left lateral, and right and left Sims. Do not position a client on an existing pressure injury or a reddened area. A 30° lateral tilt with pillows behind the back puts weight on the fleshy buttock instead of the hip bone or sacrum; place pillows between the knees and ankles so bones don't press on each other.

table.caption: Repositioning and skin-check timing at a glance
rows: Client sitting in a chair — full reposition
Client able to shift own weight

sections.example: At the bedside: A client has a Stage II injury on the sacrum and nonblanchable redness over the RIGHT hip. You're turning him off his back. Which way? A LEFT 30° lateral tilt with pillows behind the back and between the knees. That keeps weight off both the sacrum and the injured right hip. Turning onto the right side, or propping him up at 45°, would load an injured area.
sections.analogy: Think of a timer on a parking meter. In bed, the "meter" runs about 2 hours; in a chair, only about 1 hour; and a client who can move themselves should "feed the meter" every 15 minutes with a small weight shift.

sections.heading: Avoiding trauma: surfaces, head of bed, and moving the client
sections.body: The same slide on repositioning gives rules for avoiding trauma, which mostly means avoiding friction and shear.
bullets: Smooth, firm, wrinkle-free surfaces. Wrinkles, crumbs, tubing, and stacks of folded pads or blankets create ridges that dig into skin. Use one breathable pad, not several.
Correct positioning, transferring, and turning. Poor technique is itself a risk factor.
HOB ≤ 30° when possible for bedridden clients to reduce shear. Above 30°, the body slides toward the foot of the bed. Raising the knee gatch slightly also helps stop sliding.
Use draw sheets or lifts — never drag. Two staff lift the client with a draw sheet so skin does not scrape along the bed.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client on continuous tube feedings is at high risk for pressure injury. Tube feedings need the HOB raised to prevent aspiration, but a high HOB causes shear. The best balance: HOB at 30° with the knee gatch slightly raised, and reposition at least every 2 hours. Lying flat would risk aspiration; 60° would cause shear; turning every 4 hours is not often enough.

check.q: Why is "HOB 30° or lower" a pressure-injury rule?
check.a: Above about 30°, gravity pulls the body down the bed while the sacral skin sticks to the sheet — shear that tears deep blood vessels.

sections.heading: Prevention pillar 4: Supportive devices — spread the weight out
sections.body:
The goal of every support device is to keep external pressure below capillary pressure (32 mm Hg) so blood can keep flowing. The evidence on your slide is encouraging: support surfaces reduce pressure injuries by about 60%.

Types of devices:
bullets: Overlay mattresses — foam or gel placed on top of a standard bed.
Specialty beds — low-air-loss, high-air-loss, and kinetic therapy beds. Air-based beds redistribute pressure and help keep skin cooler and drier; kinetic beds slowly rotate the client.
Pillows, wedges, and heel protectors — offload specific pressure points. Place a pillow under the calves so the heels "float" off the mattress, and keep knees and ankles from resting on each other.

AVOID doughnut (ring) devices. They seem logical — lift the sore spot up — but the ring presses hard on the tissue around it, cutting off blood flow to the very center it was meant to protect. They cause injury.
sections.analogy: A support surface works like snowshoes. Your weight is the same, but spreading it over a larger area keeps you from sinking in. A doughnut cushion is the opposite — it concentrates weight on a narrow ring, like standing on the rim of a bucket.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client was just placed on a low-air-loss mattress. A new nurse says, "Now I can turn her every 4 hours instead of every 2." That statement needs correction. A support surface adds to turning — it never replaces it. Skin inspection continues, and only one breathable pad should be under the client so the air flow isn't blocked.

sections.heading: Putting prevention together: sitting clients and home caregivers
sections.body:
Clients who sit much of the day need special attention because pressure is concentrated on the ischial tuberosities. Reposition at least every hour, cue or teach weight shifts about every 15 minutes, use a pressure-redistributing seat cushion (not a ring cushion), and support the feet on the floor or a footrest so the thighs are level. Don't let the client slump or slide forward in a reclined chair — that is shear again.

At home, caregivers need clear, practical teaching: check heels, hips, and tailbone every day (a long-handled mirror helps clients check themselves), use a draw sheet with a second person, offer protein at every meal, float the heels, keep the skin clean and dry, and never use a donut pillow, massage red areas, or use powder.
sections.example: At the bedside: A 34-year-old with a T8 spinal cord injury says, "Since I can't feel my buttocks, I'll shift my weight when I start to feel uncomfortable." This needs more teaching — he can't feel the warning, so he must shift on a schedule (about every 15 minutes), not by feel. "I'll check my skin daily with a mirror" and "if a red spot doesn't fade 30 minutes after I'm off it, I'll stay off it and call the clinic" show good understanding.

mnemonics.text: Bed every 2 hours, chair every 1 hour, self weight shift every 15 minutes.

pearls: Doughnut/ring cushions are ALWAYS the wrong answer — they reduce blood flow and cause injury.
A specialty bed never replaces the turning schedule; a statement suggesting less turning "needs further teaching."
Chair = riskier than bed: reposition every hour, weight shift every 15 minutes.
"No hot water, no powder, no cornstarch, no petroleum" — mild cleanser, pat dry, barrier cream (dimethicone).
HOB ≤ 30° reduces shear; tube feeding needs at least 30°, so 30° with knee gatch is the balance point.
Monitor weight, albumin, hemoglobin, lymphocytes; nutrients = protein, calories, vitamins A & C, zinc, iron. Never restrict protein for a client at risk.
redFlags: Heels resting directly on the mattress in an immobile client → float them with a pillow under the calves or heel protectors now.
Client left in a chair for hours or sliding down in bed → reposition now and review the schedule.
Stacked pads or folded blankets under a high-risk client → remove extras; one smooth, breathable layer only.
Steady weight loss or falling albumin → supplements and dietitian consult.
recap: Nutrition: protein, calories, vitamins A & C, zinc, iron; monitor weight, lymphocytes, albumin, hemoglobin; supplements if compromised.
Skin: baseline Braden; inspect twice daily (hospital) or weekly (home); mild cleanser, no hot water; clean, dry, moisturized.
Use barrier creams/films (dimethicone, alcohol-free); avoid petroleum ointments, baby powder, cornstarch.
Reposition bed q2h, chair q1h; teach weight shifts q15 min.
HOB ≤ 30°, smooth wrinkle-free surfaces, draw sheets or lifts — never drag.
Devices keep pressure < 32 mm Hg: overlays, specialty beds, pillows, wedges, heel protectors; they cut injuries ~60%.
Never use doughnut devices.

checks.q: A paraplegic client sits in a wheelchair most of the day. How often should he shift his weight?
checks.a: About every 15 minutes — and he should be fully repositioned at least hourly in the chair.

checks.q: A caregiver says, "I'll put a donut pillow under his tailbone so it doesn't touch the bed." Your response?
checks.a: This needs correction — ring devices press on surrounding tissue and reduce blood flow, causing injury; use repositioning, pillows/wedges, and a pressure-redistributing surface instead.

checks.q: Which labs should you trend to evaluate nutritional status for pressure-injury prevention?
checks.a: Weight (not a lab, but trended), albumin, hemoglobin, and lymphocyte count.

checks.q: An LPN raises the HOB to 30° after lunch, uses a draw sheet with a UAP, and massages lotion into a red sacrum. Which action needs you to step in?
checks.a: Massaging the reddened sacrum — massage over bony prominences can worsen deep tissue damage.

checks.q: What pressure should support devices keep external pressure below, and why?
checks.a: About 32 mm Hg — capillary pressure — so the capillaries stay open and tissue keeps getting blood.

topics.title: The Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
topics.summary: Stage a pressure injury by the deepest tissue involved — from intact skin that stays red when pressed (Stage I) all the way to damage reaching muscle, tendon, or bone (Stage IV).
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the layers of the skin and underlying tissue that staging is based on.
Perform and interpret the blanch test to tell normal redness from a Stage I injury.
Recognize Stage I in darkly pigmented skin using color, temperature, firmness, and pain.
Picture and describe what Stages I, II, III, and IV look like at the bedside.
Stage a wound correctly by identifying the deepest tissue you can see or feel.
topics.bigPicture:
Staging is a shared language. When you document "Stage III sacral pressure injury," every nurse, provider, and dietitian knows how deep the damage goes and how serious it is. That shared picture drives the care plan, and it lets the team tell whether a wound is getting better or worse over time.

Your slides teach four stages. They move from the surface inward: first the skin is intact but damaged, then the top layers are lost, then the fat under the skin is involved, and finally the damage reaches muscle, bone, or the structures that hold them together.

The good news: staging is logical. If you know the layers of the skin and ask one question — "What is the deepest tissue I can see or feel?" — you can stage almost any wound on an exam.

keyTerms.def: The thin outer layer of skin — the protective "roof."
The thicker layer under the epidermis containing blood vessels, nerves, and collagen.
The fatty layer beneath the dermis (looks yellow and slightly lumpy when exposed).
Tissues like tendons, ligaments, and joint capsules that attach and hold muscles and bones.
Redness of the skin.
The skin turning pale/white when pressed, then refilling with color when released — shows blood can still flow.
Redness that STAYS red when pressed — the capillaries are damaged. The hallmark of Stage I.
Skin loss involving the epidermis and possibly part of the dermis — not all the way through (Stage II).
Skin loss through the entire epidermis and dermis, into deeper tissue (Stages III and IV).
Healthy, beefy-red, moist, bumpy new tissue that fills a healing wound.
Soft, moist, yellow or tan dead tissue in a wound bed.
Thick, dry, leathery, black or brown dead tissue.

sections.heading: The layers you are staging
sections.body:
Before you can stage, you need a mental picture of what lies under the skin. From the outside in: the epidermis (a thin protective layer), the dermis (thicker, with blood vessels and nerves — this is why a scrape that reaches the dermis bleeds and stings), the subcutaneous tissue (fat), and then muscle, tendons and other supporting structures, and bone.

Each stage is defined by how far down the damage goes. Stage I and II stay in the skin. Stage III reaches the fat. Stage IV reaches below the fat.
sections.analogy: Think of the tissue like a layered cake sitting on a plate. The epidermis is the thin frosting, the dermis is the first cake layer, the subcutaneous fat is the thick filling, and muscle and bone are the bottom layer and the plate. Stage I bruises the frosting without breaking it; Stage II scrapes off frosting and maybe some cake; Stage III digs down into the filling; Stage IV goes all the way to the bottom layer or the plate.

table.caption: Quick staging comparison
rows: Nonblanchable redness; darker area in dark skin
Shallow pink, moist wound or clear blister
Full thickness; fat may be visible; no muscle/bone
Bone, tendon, or muscle seen or felt

sections.heading: The blanch test: normal redness or Stage I?
sections.body:
When a client has been lying on one spot, it is normal for the skin to look pink or red when you turn them. This reactive redness is the body rushing blood back into tissue that was briefly squeezed. It fades once pressure is off.

To tell normal from damaged, do the blanch test (checking the "blanch response," which the assessment slide lists along with capillary refill). Press a finger (or a clear plastic disk) firmly on the red area for a few seconds, then release.

• If the area turns white (blanches) and then quickly refills with color, the capillaries are working. This is a normal response. Relieve pressure and recheck.
• If the area stays red when pressed, it is nonblanchable erythema. The capillaries are damaged and blood is leaking or pooling in the tissue. This is a Stage I pressure injury.

A practical rule often taught: redness that has not faded within about 30 minutes after pressure is removed is a warning sign that needs further assessment.
steps: Turn the client off the area and inspect under good lighting.
Press firmly on the red area with a finger or clear disk for a few seconds.
Release and watch: does it turn pale, then refill?
Blanches and refills → normal reactive redness; keep offloading and recheck.
Stays red → nonblanchable → Stage I; keep the client off it, document, and update the plan.

check.q: A UAP reports a client's sacrum is "red" after turning. What is your FIRST action?
check.a: Assess it yourself — check blanching, temperature, and firmness — before documenting a stage or treating it; the redness may be normal and transient.

sections.heading: Stage I — nonblanchable erythema of intact skin
sections.body:
The slide defines Stage I as nonblanchable erythema signaling potential ulceration. The key words are intact and nonblanchable: the skin is not broken, but it is damaged underneath.

What you would see: In lightly pigmented skin, a well-defined patch of pink-to-deep-red skin — often round or oval, about the size of a coin or a palm — directly over a bony prominence like the sacrum or heel. The surface looks unbroken, with no blister and no open area. When you press it, the red color stays. Compared with the skin around it, the area may feel warmer (inflammation), cooler (poor blood flow), firmer, or spongy/boggy (edema), and the client may say it is sore or tender.

In people of color: the slide notes Stage I may appear as darkening of the skin rather than redness. The area may look darker than the surrounding skin, or take on a purplish or bluish tone. Blanching is hard or impossible to see. So you rely on touch and comparison: is it warmer or cooler than nearby skin? Firmer or boggy? Does the client report pain? Use good lighting (natural or bright light) to see subtle color changes.

Stage I is the last chance to stop the injury before the skin opens. With pressure relief, it can resolve.
sections.example: At the bedside: Mr. T, who has darkly pigmented skin, has an area over his left hip that is slightly darker than the surrounding skin. What supports calling this Stage I? The area feels warmer and firmer than nearby skin, and he reports tenderness. If he said the mark had been there since childhood, it's likely a normal skin variation; if it had a clear blister, that would be Stage II; if it blanched, that argues against Stage I.

sections.heading: Stage II — partial-thickness skin loss
sections.body:
The slide defines Stage II as partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and possibly the dermis. The skin has now opened (or is about to), but the damage is shallow — it has not gone through the full thickness of the skin.

What you would see: Stage II usually looks one of two ways. (1) A blister — a raised, dome-shaped bubble filled with clear or straw-colored fluid, either still intact or broken open. (2) A shallow, open wound with a pink or red, moist, shiny base, like a skinned knee or a fresh abrasion. The wound is flat or very slightly dipped; you would not see yellow fat, and there is no deep crater. The edges are usually well defined, and the surrounding skin may be pink.

Because nerve endings in the dermis are exposed, Stage II injuries are often painful.
sections.example: At the bedside: During a skin check on a stroke client, you find an intact blister filled with clear, straw-colored fluid over the right heel, with pink skin around it. Documentation: Stage II pressure injury. A ruptured blister with a moist pink base, or a shallow pink open area on an ischium of a client who sits all day, would also be Stage II.

check.q: Is an intact, clear-fluid blister Stage I or Stage II?
check.a: Stage II — a blister means the epidermis has separated (partial-thickness loss), even if the blister hasn't broken.

sections.heading: Stage III — full-thickness loss into the fat
sections.body:
The slide defines Stage III as full-thickness skin loss involving damage or necrosis of subcutaneous tissue. The whole thickness of the skin is gone, and the damage has reached the fatty layer beneath.

What you would see: A true crater with visible depth. At the base or along the walls you may see yellow, slightly lumpy fat (adipose tissue). The bed may contain red granulation tissue, and there may be patches of yellow slough. The edges are distinct, and the wound can be deeper than it looks at the surface. What you would NOT see: muscle, tendon, or bone — those would make it Stage IV.

Depth varies with the location. Over the sacrum or buttock, where there is more fat, a Stage III wound can be quite deep. Over the heel or ankle, where there is little fat, a Stage III wound may look shallow even though it is full thickness.
sections.example: At the bedside: A coccyx wound measures 3 × 2 × 0.5 cm. The bed has red granulation tissue and visible yellow fat, with yellow slough covering about 20% of the base. No muscle, tendon, or bone is seen or felt. Stage? Stage III — fat is visible (full thickness), but nothing deeper.

sections.heading: Stage IV — down to muscle, bone, or supporting structures
sections.body:
The slide defines Stage IV as full-thickness skin loss with tissue necrosis or damage to muscle, bone, or supporting structures (such as tendons or joint capsules).

What you would see: A deep, cavernous wound. At its base you can see or feel deeper structures: dark red muscle, a shiny white or pearly tendon, or hard, white or grayish bone that you can touch with a sterile cotton-tipped applicator. The wound bed may contain slough or black eschar, drainage is often heavier, and there may be odor. Tissue may also be destroyed under the intact edges (undermining), so the wound is larger beneath the surface than it appears.

Stage IV wounds are the most serious. Exposed bone and deep tissue can become infected, and healing takes a long time.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client from a nursing home has a sacral wound. After cleansing you see a 3-cm-deep crater with red granulation along the sides, yellow fat in the upper wall, and a hard, white structure you can feel at the base with a sterile applicator. Fat alone would be Stage III, but bone makes this Stage IV. Always stage by the deepest tissue.

check.q: Undermining of 1 cm and red granulation along the walls — do these findings make a wound Stage IV?
check.a: No. They are wound features, not staging criteria. Stage IV requires muscle, bone, tendon, or other supporting structures to be seen or felt.

sections.heading: Staging strategy for exam questions
sections.body: When an exam gives you a wound description, work through these questions in order:
steps: Is the skin intact? If yes and the redness does NOT blanch (or it is a darker, warm, firm, tender area in dark skin) → Stage I.
Is there a clear-fluid blister (intact or ruptured) or a shallow, pink, moist open area with no fat visible? → Stage II.
Is it full thickness with fat (yellow adipose) visible, but no muscle, tendon, or bone? → Stage III.
Can you see or feel muscle, tendon, or bone? → Stage IV.
bullets: Stage by the deepest tissue you can see or feel — not the average appearance.
Slough and eschar tell you how to TREAT the wound (see the RYB lesson); the deepest tissue tells you the STAGE.
Blanchable redness that fades after turning is not a pressure injury.
sections.example: At the bedside: Four long-term care residents: (1) full-thickness hip wound with visible yellow fat, no muscle or bone → Stage III; (2) intact sacral skin with red area that does not blanch → Stage I; (3) shallow, moist pink wound on the elbow, no fat → Stage II; (4) deep ischial wound with exposed muscle → Stage IV.

mnemonics.name: "Red – Blister – Fat – Bone"
mnemonics.text: A quick ladder for Stages I–IV: nonblanchable RED on intact skin (I), BLISTER or shallow pink open area (II), FAT visible (III), BONE/muscle/tendon (IV).

pearls: Intact skin + nonblanchable redness = Stage I. Redness that blanches and fades = normal.
Any clear-fluid blister, intact or broken = Stage II.
See fat → Stage III. See or feel bone, tendon, or muscle → Stage IV.
In dark skin, Stage I may look like darkening (purple/bluish tones) — confirm with warmth or coolness, firmness/bogginess, and pain compared with nearby skin.
A UAP's report of "redness" means the RN assesses first — never document a stage you haven't assessed.
Undermining, granulation, and drainage describe a wound; they don't set the stage.
redFlags: A Stage I area that doesn't fade after pressure is relieved → keep the client completely off it and revise the positioning plan.
A wound that has gotten deeper (e.g., now shows fat or bone) → the plan is failing; reassess and notify the provider.
Deep (Stage III–IV) wound with fever, increasing pain, foul or purulent drainage → possible infection; report to the provider.
recap: Four stages, based on the deepest tissue involved.
Stage I: intact skin, nonblanchable erythema (darkening in people of color).
Stage II: partial thickness — epidermis ± dermis; clear blister or shallow pink moist wound.
Stage III: full thickness into subcutaneous tissue — fat may show; no muscle or bone.
Stage IV: full thickness with damage to muscle, bone, or supporting structures.
Blanch test separates normal reactive redness from Stage I.
In dark skin, use good lighting and compare temperature, firmness, and pain.

checks.q: A ruptured blister on the elbow has a moist pink base. Stage?
checks.a: Stage II — partial-thickness loss (a blister, intact or ruptured, with a shallow pink base).

checks.q: A deep sacral wound shows yellow fat and a shiny white tendon. Stage?
checks.a: Stage IV — a tendon is a supporting structure; stage by the deepest tissue.

checks.q: Which findings over a bony prominence fit Stage I? (a) nonblanchable redness on intact skin (b) darker area in dark skin (c) redness that fades 20 minutes after turning (d) warmth, firmness, and tenderness (e) clear blister
checks.a: a, b, and d. Fading redness is normal; a blister is Stage II.

checks.q: Why can't you rely on visible redness to find Stage I in darkly pigmented skin?
checks.a: Redness and blanching may not be visible; the injury may show only as darkening, so you compare temperature, firmness, and pain with surrounding skin under good light.

checks.q: A heel wound is full thickness but looks shallow; you see a little yellow fat. Stage?
checks.a: Stage III — the heel has little fat, so full-thickness wounds there can look shallow; visible fat without bone/muscle/tendon = Stage III.

topics.title: Pressure Injuries and the Nursing Process
topics.summary: Assess the skin and any wound the same way every time, choose the right nursing diagnosis, write measurable outcomes, carry out skin, infection, nutrition, and teaching interventions, and revise the plan when goals aren't met.
objectives: After this lesson you can perform a focused skin and wound assessment and document it objectively (location, size L × W × D, undermining, stage, bed color, margins, surrounding skin, drainage, infection, pain).
Choose the best nursing diagnosis from the slide list for a given client.
Write outcomes that are client-centered, measurable, and time-limited.
Carry out and delegate implementation for skin integrity, infection, nutrition, and teaching.
Evaluate progress and decide when the care plan must change.
topics.bigPicture:
The nursing process — assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation — is how you turn everything you know about pressure injuries into organized care for one real client. It keeps you from skipping steps: you don't treat before you assess, and you don't keep doing the same thing when it isn't working.

Pressure injury care is also a team effort. Assistive personnel turn and bathe clients many times a shift; LPNs may do established dressing changes; dietitians adjust nutrition. The RN holds the parts that need clinical judgment: assessing, staging, planning, teaching, and evaluating.

Many exam questions in this unit are really nursing-process questions: "What should the nurse do first?" (assess), "Which outcome is written correctly?" (measurable), "Is the plan working?" (evaluate). This lesson walks through each step.

keyTerms.def: How quickly color returns after pressing the skin; shows whether blood can flow through the area.
Raw, scraped, or rubbed-off skin (often from scratching, friction, or moisture).
A scrape that removes the surface of the skin.
Fluid in the tissue; over a pressure point it feels spongy or "boggy" and signals damage beneath the skin.
Tissue destroyed beneath the intact skin at the wound edge, creating a hidden "shelf" or pocket.
The edges of the wound — note whether they are attached, rolled, or have new pink tissue.
The skin surrounding the wound (check for redness, maceration, or breakdown).
Drainage types: clear-yellow / bloody / pink-watery / thick, cloudy pus (a sign of infection).
A measurable, client-centered, time-limited statement of what the client will achieve.
Assigning a task to another team member (LPN, UAP) while the RN stays accountable.

sections.heading: Assessment, part 1: inspect and palpate the skin
sections.body:
Begin with a risk tool — the slides name the Braden or Norton scale — so you know how high the risk is. Then look and feel.

Inspect under good lighting. Dim room light hides subtle color changes, especially in dark skin. Check every pressure area for discoloration (redness, darkening, purple or bluish tones), abrasions (scrapes), and excoriations (raw, rubbed skin, often from moisture or friction). Check the capillary refill/blanch response on any red area.

Palpate (feel) pressure areas and compare them with nearby skin:

• Temperature: warmer = inflammation (the body sending extra blood to damaged tissue); cooler = poor blood flow.
• Edema: tissue that feels spongy or boggy suggests damage beneath intact skin.

table.caption: What your hands and eyes are telling you
rows: Red area that turns white when pressed and quickly returns
Red area that stays red when pressed
Tissue damage — Stage I pressure injury

sections.example: At the bedside: A UAP tells you a client's sacrum is "red" after being turned. Your first action is to assess it yourself — blanching, temperature, firmness. Don't have the area massaged, don't chart a stage you haven't seen, and don't slap on a dressing before you know what it is. Assessment always comes first.

sections.heading: Assessment, part 2: measuring and describing a wound
sections.body:
If a pressure injury is present, the slide lists exactly what to note: location, size (L × W × D), undermining, stage, wound bed color, margins, surrounding skin, drainage, signs of infection, and pain. Doing this the same way every time lets anyone compare this week to last week.

Size: measure in centimeters. Length runs head-to-toe, width side-to-side. For depth, gently insert a sterile, moistened cotton-tipped applicator into the deepest part, mark it at skin level with your gloved fingers, and hold it against a ruler. Undermining is found by gently probing under the edges; record how far it goes and where (for example, "1.5 cm beneath the upper edge").

Wound bed color: describe by percentage — e.g., "80% red granulation, 20% yellow slough." Drainage: amount and type (serous, serosanguineous, purulent) and any odor after cleansing. Surrounding skin: intact? red? macerated? Pain: use a rating scale, including during dressing changes.

Always cleanse the wound before assessing it, so old drainage doesn't hide the true bed.
steps: Perform hand hygiene, apply clean gloves, and remove and discard the old dressing.
Change gloves and cleanse the wound (e.g., with normal saline).
Measure length (head to toe) and width (side to side) in centimeters.
Insert a sterile, moistened cotton-tipped applicator into the deepest area to measure depth.
Check beneath the wound edges for undermining and record its depth and location.
sections.example: At the bedside — good vs. poor documentation: Poor: "Large, gross wound on backside; drainage everywhere" or "Looks a little better; seems more comfortable." Good: "Sacral Stage III pressure injury, 4.2 cm (L) × 3.0 cm (W) × 1.1 cm (D). Undermining 1.5 cm beneath the upper edge. Bed 80% red granulation, 20% yellow slough. Moderate serosanguineous drainage, no odor after cleansing. Periwound skin intact without maceration. Client rates pain 3/10 during dressing change." The good entry is objective, measurable, and comparable.

sections.heading: Diagnosis: naming the client's problem
sections.body: The slide lists possible nursing diagnoses. Choosing the right one depends on whether the skin is still intact, and on what else the client is dealing with:
bullets: Potential for impaired skin integrity — the client is at risk (e.g., low Braden score) but the skin is still intact and any redness blanches.
Impaired skin integrity — damage is present (a pressure injury exists).
Risk for infection — the skin barrier is open, so bacteria have a way in.
Underweight — poor intake and weight loss that undermine skin health and healing.
Compromised dignity — wounds, odor, incontinence, and exposure during care can make a client feel embarrassed or diminished.
Situational low self-esteem — the client's view of themselves drops because of the wound and its effects (for example, avoiding visitors).
sections.example: At the bedside: A 75-year-old on bed rest has a Braden score of 12. The skin is intact, and all red areas blanch and fade after turning. Best diagnosis: Potential for impaired skin integrity — high risk, but no damage yet. Once a Stage I or deeper injury appears, the diagnosis becomes impaired skin integrity.

check.q: A client with a Stage IV wound says, "I can smell my wound. I don't want my grandkids to visit." Which two slide diagnoses fit?
check.a: Compromised dignity and situational low self-esteem (plus risk for infection and impaired skin integrity from the wound itself).

sections.heading: Planning: writing outcomes that can be measured
sections.body:
The slide lists collaborative outcomes for pressure injury care:

• Reposition every 2 hours (immobile clients) with positioning devices.
• Mobile clients maintain or improve activity levels.
• The client reports changes in skin condition (pain, redness, drainage).
• The client verbalizes the importance of nutrition and hydration.
• The client describes protective measures for the skin.

A well-written expected outcome is client-centered ("The client will…"), specific, measurable (you can see or count it), realistic, and time-limited (by when?). Watch for common errors: an outcome that describes what the nurse will do is an intervention, not an outcome; verbs like "understand" or "know" can't be observed; words like "quickly" or "better" can't be measured.

table.caption: Outcome statements — correct or not?
rows: "The client will state three ways to protect the skin before discharge."
"The sacral wound will decrease in length and width by 25% within 2 weeks."
"The client will have no new areas of nonblanchable erythema during hospitalization."
"The nurse will turn the client every 2 hours."
"The client will understand the importance of good nutrition."

sections.heading: Implementation: protecting skin integrity
sections.body: The implementation slide on skin integrity lists the core bedside actions. You already met most of them in the prevention lesson; here they are as part of the plan:
bullets: Daily skin inspection, focusing on bony areas (more often for high-risk clients).
Gentle cleansing with mild agents; avoid hot water.
Moisturize dry skin.
Manage moisture from incontinence, sweat, and wound drainage (prompt cleansing, barrier cream).
Avoid massage over bony prominences. Rubbing damaged tissue can break fragile capillaries and worsen deep injury.
Use proper turning, transferring, and positioning techniques (draw sheet or lift, never drag).
Reposition every 2 hours in bed; every 1 hour in a chair; teach weight shifting every 15 minutes.
sections.analogy: Massaging a reddened bony prominence is like rubbing a bruise hard to "make it go away" — you're pressing on tissue that's already damaged and making the bleeding underneath worse.

sections.heading: Implementation: infection, nutrition, teaching, and who does what
sections.body:
Preventing infection: good hygiene (hand hygiene, clean skin, clean dressings), adequate hydration, early recognition of infection, and reporting changes to the health care provider (HCP). Signs that a wound may be infected include increasing pain, spreading redness and warmth, purulent (pus-like) or foul-smelling drainage, fever, and a rising white blood cell count. If the provider orders a wound culture and antibiotics, the culture is collected before the first antibiotic dose.

Nutrition: assess intake (e.g., percent of meals eaten), provide supplements, and consult the dietitian if needed.

Teaching clients and caregivers: pressure injury risk factors; skin care and positioning; the importance of diet and hydration; and dressing changes and wound care if applicable.

Who does what: the RN keeps assessment, staging, care planning, the teaching plan, and evaluation. UAP can turn and reposition, bathe, give incontinence care, help with meals, and report redness or other changes. An LPN can perform an established, prescribed dressing change for a stable client whose wound the RN has already assessed and staged, collect data, and reinforce teaching.
sections.example: At the bedside: In hand-off you receive four clients. Who first? A Stage II with a rolled dressing edge; a Braden 12 client last turned 2½ hours ago; a Stage III due for a routine dressing change; or a Stage IV client who is newly confused with HR 116 and BP 88/50? See the Stage IV client first — new confusion, tachycardia, and low blood pressure suggest a spreading, body-wide infection from the wound. Delegate the overdue turn to the UAP.

check.q: Which task is most appropriate for an LPN: (a) admission skin assessment and staging, (b) the prescribed dressing change on a Stage III wound the RN staged today, (c) writing a discharge teaching plan, (d) staging a new heel wound?
check.a: (b) — an established procedure on a stable, already-assessed client. The others need RN assessment or planning.

sections.heading: Evaluation: is the plan working?
sections.body:
Evaluation closes the loop. The slide tells you to reassess skin integrity daily (or more often if high risk) and evaluate:

• Skin healing — are wounds getting smaller and shallower, with more red granulation and new pink tissue at the edges?
• Comfort and pain control.
• Repositioning schedule compliance — is the turning actually happening?
• Nutritional intake — percent of meals, supplements taken, weight trend.

If goals are not met, modify the care plan. Signs a wound is deteriorating: larger or deeper measurements, increasing undermining, new or increasing slough or eschar, more or purulent drainage, odor, or maceration of the surrounding skin. A pressure injury that shows no progress over about 2 weeks also calls for re-evaluation. Finally, mobile clients are taught to report new pressure areas themselves.
sections.example: At the bedside: Day 7 after starting a prevention plan: sacral redness now blanches and fades within 30 minutes (effective); the left heel blister has reabsorbed and the skin is intact (effective); the client eats 75% of meals plus two supplements (effective); but the left ischial wound is now 0.4 cm deep with visible fat, and there is a new area of nonblanchable redness over the left hip (ineffective). The nurse reassesses positioning, the support surface, and turning technique, and revises the plan.

pearls: "First action" after a report of redness = the RN assesses (blanch test, temperature, firmness).
Objective documentation uses cm, percentages, drainage type/amount, and pain scores — never "looks better."
Intact skin + high risk = Potential for impaired skin integrity; any injury = Impaired skin integrity.
Outcomes start with "The client will…," are measurable, and have a time frame; "the nurse will…" is an intervention.
UAP turn, bathe, and report; LPN does established dressing changes on stable clients; RN assesses, stages, plans, teaches, evaluates.
Acknowledge feelings about wounds and odor ("You sound embarrassed — let's plan…"), then solve the problem with the client.
redFlags: Wound getting larger or deeper, new slough/eschar, odor, or purulent drainage → reassess and revise the plan; notify the provider.
New confusion, fever, tachycardia, or hypotension in a client with a deep pressure injury → possible spreading infection; assess first and report immediately.
Any new nonblanchable redness during a prevention plan → the plan isn't working; change positioning/surface.
recap: Assess: risk tool (Braden/Norton), inspect under good light, check blanch response, palpate temperature and edema.
Document wounds: location, L × W × D in cm, undermining, stage, bed color %, margins, surrounding skin, drainage, infection signs, pain.
Diagnoses: potential for / impaired skin integrity, risk for infection, underweight, compromised dignity, situational low self-esteem.
Outcomes: client-centered, measurable, time-limited.
Implement: daily inspection, gentle cleansing, moisturize, manage moisture, no massage, proper turning (bed q2h, chair q1h, shift q15 min).
Also: infection prevention, nutrition support, and teaching; delegate appropriately.
Evaluate daily; modify the plan if goals aren't met.

checks.q: Put in order: measure depth, remove old dressing, check undermining, cleanse, measure L × W.
checks.a: Remove old dressing → cleanse → measure L × W → measure depth → check undermining.

checks.q: Tissue is destroyed 2 cm beneath the intact skin at the lower wound edge. What is this called?
checks.a: Undermining — document its depth and location (e.g., "2 cm at the lower edge").

checks.q: Is "The nurse will reposition the client every 2 hours" an outcome?
checks.a: No — it describes a nurse action (an intervention). Outcomes describe what the client will achieve.

checks.q: Which task can the RN delegate to a UAP: completing the Braden scale, staging a wound, or turning the client every 2 hours and reporting redness?
checks.a: Turning and reporting redness. The Braden assessment and staging need RN judgment.

checks.q: A Stage III wound is larger and deeper than last week, with more slough. What does the nurse conclude and do?
checks.a: The wound is deteriorating; the plan isn't working. Reassess the client and wound and collaborate with the team to revise the plan.

topics.title: Wound Care: The RYB Color Guide & Debridement
topics.summary: Let the color of the wound bed guide your care — protect red, cleanse yellow, debride black — and know the five ways dead tissue can be removed and which ones the nurse can do.
objectives: After this lesson you can identify red, yellow, and black wound tissue and state the treatment goal for each.
Decide which color to treat first in a mixed wound.
Explain why dead tissue must be removed for a wound to heal.
Describe sharp, mechanical, chemical, autolytic, and maggot (biosurgery) debridement and who performs each.
Recognize when a debridement order (such as wet-to-dry on a clean red wound) should be clarified.
topics.bigPicture:
When you look into an open pressure injury, the colors you see tell you what's happening inside. Healthy, healing tissue is red. Dead tissue that is soft and stringy is yellow. Dead tissue that has dried into a hard crust is black. The RYB (red–yellow–black) color guide turns those colors into simple treatment goals.

Why does color matter so much? Dead tissue is like garbage in the wound. It gives bacteria a place to grow, it releases substances that slow healing, and it physically blocks new tissue from filling in. A wound cannot heal while it is full of dead tissue. So the nurse's job is to protect healthy tissue and help get rid of dead tissue — in the right way.

This lesson teaches you to read wound colors, choose the right goal, and understand the ways dead tissue is removed (called debridement) and what part the nurse plays in each.

keyTerms.def: A wound-care system: Red = protect, Yellow = cleanse, Black = debride.
Healthy, beefy-red, moist, bumpy new tissue full of tiny blood vessels; it bleeds easily.
Soft, moist, stringy yellow (or tan) dead tissue in the wound bed.
Thick, dry, leathery black or brown dead tissue.
Tissue that is dead and cannot recover.
Removal of dead (necrotic) or nonviable tissue from a wound so it can heal.
Cutting away dead tissue with a scalpel — performed by a surgeon.
Physically pulling dead tissue off — on your slides, with a wet-to-dry dressing.
Applying a prescribed enzyme product that dissolves dead tissue.
Using special dressings that trap the wound's own drainage so the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue.
Placing sterile maggots on a nonhealing necrotic wound; they digest dead tissue with minimal harm to healthy tissue.
Removes healthy tissue along with dead tissue (wet-to-dry is nonselective).

sections.heading: Why dead tissue has to go
sections.body:
A pressure injury heals from the bottom up and the edges in. New granulation tissue grows up from the wound bed, and new skin creeps in from the edges. For that to happen, the wound bed needs to be clean and alive.

Necrotic (dead) tissue gets in the way in three ways: it is a food source for bacteria, raising infection risk; it physically blocks new tissue from growing; and it hides how deep the wound really is. That is why the RYB guide focuses so much on getting rid of yellow and black tissue.
sections.analogy: Healing a wound full of dead tissue is like trying to plant a new lawn on top of old trash. Until you clear the trash away, the grass can't take root — and the trash attracts pests (bacteria).

sections.heading: Red — PROTECT
sections.body:
What it looks like: a beefy red, moist, shiny wound bed with a slightly bumpy, "cobblestone" texture — like the inside of a ripe strawberry or raw ground beef. This is granulation tissue, packed with brand-new tiny blood vessels. It may bleed slightly when touched. At the edges you may see a thin rim of new pink skin creeping inward.

Goal: PROTECT. Red is good — it means healing. This tissue is fragile, so the goal is to protect it from trauma and keep it moist. Don't scrub it, and don't use anything that will stick to it and tear it off when removed.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client's sacral wound has a beefy red, moist bed with no slough, eschar, odor, or signs of infection. He asks why you aren't "scrubbing it clean." You explain that this is healthy healing tissue, so the goal is to protect it and keep it moist; scrubbing would damage the new tissue.

sections.heading: Yellow — CLEANSE
sections.body:
What it looks like: soft, moist, yellow, cream, or tan tissue that may be stringy (like wet threads or strands of melted cheese) or form a film over the wound bed. This is slough — nonviable tissue mixed with wound drainage. It may be loosely attached or stuck to the bed. Yellow wounds often have more drainage.

Goal: CLEANSE to remove the nonviable tissue. The slough needs to come off so the red tissue underneath can grow. Careful: yellow slough is not the same as yellow fat (subcutaneous tissue) you might see in a Stage III wound. Fat is living, lumpy, and part of the wound wall; slough is a soft film or strands of dead material.

check.q: Soft, stringy yellow nonviable tissue covers a wound bed. What's the RYB goal?

sections.heading: Black — DEBRIDE
sections.body:
What it looks like: a thick, dry, hard, leathery patch that is black or dark brown, like a thick scab or a piece of burnt leather. This is eschar — dead tissue that has dried out. It may be firmly stuck to the wound bed with edges lifting at the sides.

Goal: DEBRIDE. Eschar must be removed for healing to occur. The slide adds an important note: nurses can debride, but with limitations — some methods are nursing actions (with a prescription), and some are performed by a surgeon.
sections.example: At the bedside: A sacral wound has 40% black eschar, 40% yellow slough, and 20% red granulation. Which goal comes first? Debride the black. In a mixed wound, address the least healthy tissue first: black → yellow → red. Necrotic tissue blocks healing of the whole wound.

table.caption: RYB color guide at a glance
rows: Beefy red, moist, bumpy; bleeds easily

sections.heading: The five ways to debride — and who does each
sections.body: Debridement means removing dead tissue. The slides list five forms. Each needs a provider's prescription; the difference is who carries it out and how selective it is (whether it removes only dead tissue or healthy tissue too).

table.caption: Debridement methods from the slides
rows: Dead tissue is cut away with a scalpel
Wet-to-dry dressing: moist gauze dries in the wound and pulls tissue off when removed
Nonselective — removes healthy tissue too; painful
Prescribed enzymes applied to dissolve necrotic tissue
Special dressings capture/hold drainage so the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue
Slowest, gentlest; uses the body's own processes
Sterile maggots placed on the wound digest damaged tissue
Minimal harm to healthy tissue; for nonhealing necrotic wounds

check.q: Fill in: "_____ debridement uses a wet-to-dry dressing; _____ debridement is done by a surgeon with a scalpel; _____ debridement uses special dressings and the body's own enzymes."

sections.heading: A closer look: wet-to-dry (mechanical) debridement
sections.body:
A wet-to-dry dressing is gauze moistened (usually with saline) and placed into the wound. As it dries, it grabs onto whatever tissue it touches. When the nurse removes the dry gauze, that tissue comes off with it.

The problem: the gauze can't tell dead tissue from healthy tissue. That makes wet-to-dry nonselective. It pulls off slough and eschar, but also any healthy red granulation tissue it has stuck to — and removal is painful. That's why it belongs only in wounds that actually contain dead tissue to remove.
sections.example: At the bedside: The provider orders wet-to-dry dressings every 6 hours for a Stage III wound. You find the bed is 100% red granulation with scant serous drainage. You clarify the order before doing it, because wet-to-dry is nonselective and would strip the healthy granulation tissue that the RYB guide says to protect.
sections.analogy: Wet-to-dry is like pulling off a bandage that has dried into a scraped knee — it takes the scab, but it also rips away the fresh new skin underneath.

sections.heading: A closer look: biosurgery (maggot therapy)
sections.body:
It sounds surprising, but it's real medicine. In biosurgery, sterile maggots (fly larvae raised in a lab so they carry no germs) are placed on a nonhealing wound that contains necrotic tissue. The maggots digest the damaged, dead tissue and do minimal damage to the surrounding healthy tissue. According to your slides, in some cases biosurgery is preferable to surgical debridement of necrotic wounds.

Clients are often nervous or disgusted at first, so teaching matters. Key points: the larvae are sterile, they target dead tissue, they are removed after treatment (they don't stay in the wound permanently), and the rest of the care plan — including pressure relief — continues.
sections.example: At the bedside: A client with a nonhealing Stage IV heel wound full of necrotic tissue is scheduled for biosurgery. Which statement shows understanding? "The larvae digest dead tissue and do little harm to healthy tissue." Statements like "they'll eat healthy tissue too," "they stay until the wound closes," or "I don't have to keep pressure off my heel anymore" need more teaching.

sections.heading: Putting it together: the nurse's role and watching for infection
sections.body:
Your wound-care job, step by step: assess the wound (after cleansing) and estimate the percentage of each color; set the goal from the RYB guide; carry out the prescribed care — protecting red tissue, cleansing slough, and performing the debridement methods within the nurse's role (mechanical, chemical, autolytic) — and clarify any order that doesn't match the wound. Sharp debridement is done by the surgeon.

Keep watching for infection, which is more likely in wounds that contain dead tissue: increasing pain, spreading redness and warmth, purulent or foul-smelling drainage, fever, and a rising WBC. Report these changes to the provider. If a wound culture and antibiotics are ordered, collect the culture before the first antibiotic dose. Track response by trending the temperature, the marked border of redness, and the drainage.

Remember that debridement treats the wound, not the cause. Repositioning, support surfaces, moisture control, and nutrition must continue or the wound will not heal.
steps: Cleanse the wound, then assess: size, stage, and % red / yellow / black.
Pick the goal: black → debride; yellow → cleanse; red → protect.
Match the prescribed method to the goal; clarify any order that would harm healthy tissue.
Perform nurse-appropriate care (mechanical, chemical, autolytic as prescribed); sharp debridement goes to the surgeon.
Watch for infection and report changes; keep up pressure relief and nutrition.
Re-evaluate: is the black and yellow shrinking and the red growing?

mnemonics.name: RYB = "Protect, Clean, Debride" (like a traffic light for wounds)
mnemonics.text: Red = protect (keep moist); Yellow = cleanse (remove slough); Black = debride (remove eschar). Mixed wound? Treat the worst color first: black → yellow → red.

pearls: Red protect, yellow cleanse, black debride — memorize it cold.
Mixed-color wound: treat the least healthy tissue first (black, then yellow, then red).
Sharp debridement with a scalpel = surgeon. Mechanical, chemical, and autolytic are done by the nurse with a prescription.
Wet-to-dry is nonselective — it pulls off healthy tissue. Clarify a wet-to-dry order for a clean, 100% red wound.
Maggots eat dead tissue, not healthy tissue — and pressure relief still continues.
Don't confuse yellow slough (dead) with yellow fat (living subcutaneous tissue, Stage III clue).
redFlags: Purulent, foul-smelling drainage with spreading redness, warmth, fever, or rising WBC → possible wound infection; report to the provider (culture before antibiotics if ordered).
New black eschar or increasing slough in a previously clean wound → the wound is deteriorating; reassess and revise the plan.
Wet-to-dry ordered on a clean granulating wound → hold and clarify with the provider.
recap: Dead tissue feeds bacteria and blocks healing, so it must be removed.
Red (granulation) = protect and keep moist.
Yellow (slough) = cleanse to remove nonviable tissue.
Black (eschar) = debride; nurses can debride with limitations.
Debridement methods: sharp (surgeon, scalpel), mechanical (wet-to-dry), chemical (enzymes), autolytic (special dressings that capture drainage), maggots (biosurgery).
Wet-to-dry is nonselective; biosurgery is selective for dead tissue.
Mixed wound: black → yellow → red.

checks.q: A wound is covered with thick, dry, black, leathery tissue. RYB goal?
checks.a: Debride — eschar must be removed for healing.

checks.q: Which debridement method is outside the nurse's role: enzyme ointment, wet-to-dry, autolytic dressing, or scalpel removal?
checks.a: Scalpel removal (sharp debridement) — performed by a surgeon.

checks.q: Why should the nurse question a wet-to-dry order for a wound that is 100% red granulation?
checks.a: Wet-to-dry is nonselective; as it dries it sticks to all tissue and removal tears off healthy granulation. Red wounds should be protected.

checks.q: A client getting maggot therapy says, "Now I don't have to keep pressure off my heel." Correct?
checks.a: No — biosurgery removes dead tissue, but pressure relief and other wound care must continue.

checks.q: Clean wound with pink granulation and a new pink rim at the edges. RYB goal?
checks.a: Protect — it's healthy, healing tissue; keep it moist and free from trauma.
